chunks: "Open loop, an op-amp has no feedback to hold the inputs together, so its enormous gain acts on any difference.
If the plus input is even a hundred microvolts above the minus input, the output slams to the positive rail.
If it's below, it goes to the negative rail, or ground in a single-supply design. So it behaves like a comparator: it compares two voltages and outputs a one or a zero.
There's a tiny linear region, about the supply voltage divided by the gain, so a couple hundred microvolts wide, and it isn't useful.
The circuit type is a comparator, essentially a one-bit analog-to-digital converter. It's used for threshold detection, zero-crossing detectors, and PWM generation.
The catch is noise. If the input hovers near the threshold, even millivolts of noise make the output chatter back and forth.
The fix is hysteresis: feed a bit of the output back to the plus input through a resistor, which is positive feedback.
That's a Schmitt trigger, with two thresholds, one for rising and one for falling inputs. And I'd mention that general-purpose op-amps aren't great comparators.
They recover slowly from saturation, some have input clamp diodes, and the output isn't logic level. A dedicated comparator IC is faster and designed for this."
